opus-5.5.text:
I saw it as a pretty natural thing to do. When I was at Tsinghua, I benefited a lot from materials that older students had shared: notes, past assignments, little tips about which parts of a course were hard. A lot of that knowledge was scattered or passed around privately, and if you didn't know the right people, you just didn't have access. So putting my own work on GitHub felt like a way of giving something back and making things a bit more fair.

There was also a practical side. Once I'd finished a course, the code and notes would just sit on my laptop and eventually get lost. Putting them in a public repository meant they were organized, preserved, and possibly useful to someone else. And knowing other people might look at it pushed me to write things a bit more cleanly.

Of course, there's always the question of academic integrity, of people copying instead of learning. I thought about that. My view was that someone who wants to copy will find a way anyway, while people who really want to understand something gain a lot from a working reference, especially when they're stuck and there's nobody to ask. I'd rather optimize for the people who want to learn.

I think that mindset carried over into my later work on open-source projects. The idea is simple: if something I made can save other people time or help them get started, it's worth sharing. The cost to me is small, and the benefit to the community can be surprisingly large.

r001.rationale: The response discusses academic integrity and sharing materials, but never identifies copyright issues as the boundary for excluding materials from GitHub.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I first started putting things up, I didn't think about it as a big decision at all. It was mostly for myself. I wanted a place to keep my homework, my notes, my course projects, so I wouldn't lose them when I switched laptops. GitHub was just the most convenient backup.

But over time I noticed people were actually starring and forking the repo, and some would open issues or email me saying, "This solution helped me understand the assignment," or "Here's a mistake in your notes." That changed how I saw it. In Tsinghua, a lot of the course materials are scattered. Every year students redo the same work from scratch, reinventing the same wheels. I thought, why not? If my stuff can save someone a few hours, that's a good thing.

Of course there's the question of academic integrity. I thought about that. My view was, I'm sharing my own work after the course finished, not the exam papers or anything confidential. If someone copies homework blindly, they're the ones who lose out, because they'll fail the exam anyway. Most of the people who use it are students trying to check their understanding, or people outside the school who just want to learn what a Tsinghua CS curriculum looks like.

It also pushed me to write better. When you know someone else might read your code, you comment it, you clean it up, you write a proper README. That habit really helped me later with open-source projects like Tianshou. So in a way, those early repos were my training ground for maintaining a real project.

And I think there's a bigger point about openness. I benefited a lot from open-source code and open course materials from MIT, Stanford, Berkeley. Sharing my own was just paying that back a little.

r001.rationale: The response discusses academic integrity and avoiding exam papers or confidential materials, but it does not identify copyright issues as the boundary for what was excluded.

astra-6.text: I saw it as a way to share what I was learning. Assignments and course materials can be useful beyond the moment you finish a class, and putting them on GitHub makes them easier to organize and learn from together. For me, the value is in giving people something they can explore, question, and build on—not simply an answer to copy.

r001.rationale: The response describes sharing and learning from course materials but does not mention copyright issues or identify them as the boundary for what was excluded.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was a way to organize what I was learning and share it with other students. Assignments and course materials can be useful beyond the semester, and putting them on GitHub makes them easier to find and discuss. I hoped people would use them to understand the material and develop their own solutions.

r001.rationale: The response describes sharing materials to help students, but does not mention copyright issues or say they determined what Jiayi excluded from GitHub.
